name: Comecrudo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1887. Ethnologic results obtained upon an expedition in the south-west of the United States. Science 9(221): 411-413 (letter to the compilers dated 29 April 1887; first-hand: Gatschet recorded Comecrudo at Las Prietas near Camargo, Tamaulipas, in 1886).
catalog_locator: p. 412, right column, paragraph beginning 'From Laredo, Webb county, Tex., I went south to Camargo'
catalog_quote: The pronunciation of these Indians is remarkably clear, and only a few words contain nasal sounds. The language is lacking the sounds f, r, tch, dsh, ts, ds, b, and d, but diphthongs are frequent. Only two tenses are extant, but the noun is inflected by some cases of a locative character. A demonstrative particle, pa- or pe-, is found before almost every noun, and in some verbs also. There is also a tendency to oxytonize many words, especially substantives, although the accent shifts, as in other Indian languages.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent tends to fall on the final syllable (oxytone), especially in nouns; the accent is not rigidly fixed and may shift. Corroborated second-hand by Zamponi 2024: 123 ('Stress usually falls on the last syllable'; paroxytone and proparoxytone words uncommon) and by the distribution of Gatschet's accent marks in Swanton 1940 (c. 78% of polysyllabic headwords marked on the final syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Gatschet: the tendency holds 'especially' for substantives and 'the accent shifts'; Zamponi (snippet): paroxytone and proparoxytone words exist but are 'apparently.. uncommon', e.g. pékla 'suck', máwayo 'singer or dancer'.
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic fieldworker remark (1886 elicitation through Spanish from elderly rememberers; language already moribund) about isolated words/citation forms; 'accent shifts' is not explained (presumably in connected speech or under affixation). No phonological analysis exists beyond philological interpretation of Gatschet's notes.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement concerns Comecrudo proper ('Carrizo' of the lower Rio Grande) as remembered by Gatschet's three consultants (Emiterio, Joaquin, Andrade) at Las Prietas near Camargo, Tamaulipas, in 1886 -- the variety behind ISO xcm. Glottolog 5.1 labels come1251 'Comecrudan' at language level; the related Garza and Mamulique wordlists (Berlandier 1828-29) are not covered by the statement. The language was moribund when recorded (elicitation through Spanish; 'none of his informants seeming to have had a fluent command of it', Swanton 1940: 4) and is extinct; every later description (Swanton 1940, Kaufman 1973, Goddard 1979, Zamponi 2024) is philological interpretation of Gatschet's notes.

new_statements.quote: Stress usually falls on the last syllable. Paroxitone and proparoxitone words like, apparently, the following are uncommon: pékla ‘suck’, máwayo ‘singer or dancer’, akikéte ‘swim’, anawéwayi ‘little’. A few suffixes are unstressed: pam-kám-e ‘medicine’, pa-kaí-la ‘eatable’, pai-kió-kam ‘Do you wish to walk?’; see also example (46) below.
new_statements.citation: Zamponi, Raoul. 2024. Extinct lineages and unclassified languages of Mexico. In Søren Wichmann (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mexico and Northern Central America (The World of Linguistics 12?), 99-158. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. Comecrudo section, phonology c. p. 123.
new_statements.locator: p. 123 (PDF page 25 of 60), Comecrudo phonology paragraph following Tab. 10 'Tentative consonantal system of Comecrudo'; unstressed-suffix examples continue in example (46), p. 124
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 60 pages, native text (extracted text, no scanned). The quoted passage is on printed p. 123 (PDF page 25, running header 'Extinct lineages and unclassified languages of Mexico 123'), the third paragraph after Tab. 10 'Tentative consonantal system of Comecrudo', exactly as quoted: 'Stress usually falls on the last syllable. Paroxitone and proparoxitone words like, apparently, the following are uncommon: pékla ‘suck’, máwayo ‘singer or dancer’, akikéte ‘swim’, anawéwayi ‘little’. A few suffixes are unstressed: pam-kám-e ‘medicine’, pa-kaí-la ‘eatable’, pai-kió-kam ‘Do you wish to walk?’; see also example (46) below.' Example (46) on p. 124 (PDF page 26) confirmed: pa-kaí-le ‘is going to eat’…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed-unreviewed, final-syllable final stress) and as the existing statement from Gatschet 1887 ('tendency to oxytonize many words.. although the accent shifts'). Zamponi adds detail: final stress is the usual pattern rather than exceptionless, paroxytones/proparoxytones are uncommon, and certain suffixes are unstressed so that stress falls on the last syllable of the stem. Compatible with the catalog placement; the hedge 'usually' and the unstressed-suffix note could justify a 'refines' label as well, but the placement itself is unchanged.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress normally falls on the final syllable of the word; penultimate and antepenultimate stress occur but are uncommon. A few suffixes (-e, -la, -kam, -le) are inherently unstressed, so stress stays on the last syllable of the stem/root rather than on the suffix; i.e. final stress is counted over the stem, not the fully suffixed word.
new_statements.exceptions: Paroxytone and proparoxytone words exist but are 'uncommon': pékla 'suck', máwayo 'singer or dancer', akikéte 'swim', anawéwayi 'little'. Unstressed suffixes: pam-kám-e 'medicine', pa-kaí-la 'eatable', pai-kió-kam 'Do you wish to walk?', and the -le forms in example (46) p. 124 (pa-kaí-le 'is going to eat', pa-kám-le 'I wish to drink', pa-klehuén-le 'to thunder', p-eháp-le 'fallen'). The author cautions (p. 122) that the phonology is obscured by the recorders' orthographies; all examples are Gatschet's 1886 material as published by Swanton 1940.
new_statements.identity_note: Zamponi's Comecrudo data are Gatschet's 1886 field material from three descendants of the last speakers at Las Prietas (Tamaulipas), published by Swanton 1940; the same locality as Gatschet 1887. Garza and Mamulique (the other Comecrudan languages) are discussed in the same section only for lexical comparison, with no stress statement. The stress statement concerns Comecrudo proper only.

sources.note: No stress rule. p. 10: 'The accents in Comecrudo, Cotoname, and the Karankawa recorded by Dr. Gatschet are as given by the last named investigator.' Gatschet's accent mark (written after the stressed vowel) appears on nearly every Comecrudo form; my crude tally of 611 accented headwords: final 436, penult 103, antepenult 18, monosyllables 54 (unpublished note).
